routes.description: Establish that religious belief better secures moral knowledge and social judgment by grounding durable duties in divine authority and by showing that religious traditions can identify grave public evils more reliably than secular institutions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine authorship is given an adequate basis, transcendent authority explains the stability of binding duties, and the practical record supports religion's comparative capacity to recognize evil and sustain a good society.

motionBridge.description: Show that divine authority provides a firmer basis for moral knowledge and recognition of social evil than secular ethical deliberation provides.

centralBridges.description: Provide grounds for believing in an intentional creator and for treating sacred teaching as a credible source of moral authority.
Explain why divine authority makes core prohibitions binding and durable despite fallible human preferences and disagreement.
Show that a worldview's moral adequacy is tested by its capacity to identify major evils and contribute to a good society.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how disputed ancient rules may represent moral advances when interpreted within their historical setting.
Support the comparative claim that religious communities can recognize ideologically motivated evil that secular institutions overlook.

routes.description: Establish that secular ethical realism can guide moral knowledge and progress through evidence about conscious experience, rational inquiry, cooperation, and revisable public reasoning without relying on supernatural authorship or sacred authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if wellbeing and suffering furnish defensible moral facts, rational inquiry explains moral convergence and correction, and religious dogma is shown to be unnecessary or obstructive in identifying and remedying social evil.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular ethical realism can ground moral knowledge and moral progress without supernatural premises or sacred texts.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral distinctions in facts about the happiness, suffering, capacities, and relationships of conscious creatures.
Explain how open-ended rational inquiry can discover, test, and revise moral rules while distinguishing evidence-based realism from pragmatism.
Show how unsupported supernatural or political dogmas can motivate violence and obstruct effective moral judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how attachment, reciprocity, mutual care, and viable social cooperation support prohibitions such as the rule against murder.
Show how secular analysis can make morally relevant distinctions among forms and stages of conscious life.

sections.title: Moral Authority and Binding Obligation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether durable moral duties require divine command or can arise from rationally accessible facts about persons, cooperation, harm, and flourishing.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge and Ethical Realism
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require an account of how moral claims become knowable, objective, corrigible, and distinguishable from preference or mere practical success.

sections.title: Creator, Scripture, and Dogmatic Authority
sections.rationale: The status of a creator and sacred texts matters because the pro route invokes them as foundations while the con route challenges their evidentiary basis and moral reliability.

sections.title: Recognizing Social Evil and Testing Worldviews
sections.rationale: The debate uses communism, fascism, religious extremism, and institutional judgment to test which framework better identifies dangerous ideologies and supports moral progress.

sections.title: Consciousness, Human Status, and Contested Cases
sections.rationale: Disputes involving human uniqueness, animals, embryos, fetuses, suffering, and development test how each framework draws and justifies morally significant boundaries.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Claims that sacred books were written or informed by a supernatural creator are unsupported and dangerously divisive, particularly because they obstruct rational responses to religious extremism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager directly invites Harris to characterize his view, and Harris delivers the ensuing first-person explanation without attribution ambiguity.

response.rationale: This is a constructive challenge to supernatural authorship and its alleged harmful consequences, so no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a central challenge but compresses the evidentiary support for its broad consequences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but claims about divisiveness, danger, and the Muslim world broaden beyond the specifically stated supernatural premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt confidently calls the dogma uniquely dangerous and unsupported without supplying comparative evidence for that breadth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unsupported supernatural authorship to dangerous divisiveness is intelligible but leaves a material causal bridge underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The factual and comparative claims rely largely on assertion and a reference to conflict in the Muslim world rather than representative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central dogma-and-harm bridge, though it does not complete the broader secular-grounding route.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is examined closely enough for a meaningful charity test in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly labels supernatural scriptural authorship unsupported, divisive, dangerous, and costly in relation to the Muslim world.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Religious Americans are more likely than secular academics to recognize the threat of Islamic totalitarianism, supporting a comparative claim that religiosity can sharpen rather than impede the identification of grave social evil.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly speaks in the first person, identifies himself among religious Americans, and develops the challenge addressed to Harris.

components.text: Whether religion obstructs recognition of religious extremism and its associated social danger.
Whether supernatural scriptural claims themselves are evidentially supported.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the claimed practical obstruction by alleging superior religious recognition of Islamic totalitarianism, but it does not answer the unsupported-authorship component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that reaches the decisive practical-harm component while leaving the supernatural-evidence challenge untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is clear, but categories such as evangelical leaders, secular professors, and religious Americans shift without a stated sampling scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A broad comparative likelihood is asserted from an acknowledged example without documentation, base rates, or qualification about populations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample bears on practical discernment, but one comparative instance does not establish that religiosity generally sharpens recognition of evil.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The population comparison and designation of the greatest moral threat are asserted without representative evidence or rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports religious discernment, a subsidiary bridge, and does so near the upper part of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a contrary example but does not develop or characterize a strongest alternative interpretation in enough detail to test charity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager contrasts evangelical Christian leaders with secular academic professors in recognizing Islamic totalitarianism as a major threat.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: When martyrdom, jihad, and immediate paradise are accepted as true religious premises, catastrophic violence can be internally rational, and religious believers may recognize that motivational logic particularly clearly.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris begins with an explicit concession and then explains, in a continuous response, why religious observers recognize the motivating beliefs.

components.text: Why religious observers may recognize the motivating logic of Islamic totalitarian violence.
Whether religious Americans are comparatively more likely than secular academics to recognize the threat.

response.rationale: Harris explains recognition through familiarity with the logical consequences of religious premises, contacting the recognition point while not establishing the population comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The partial answer reaches the decisive explanatory component but leaves the asserted comparative frequency largely untested.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on accepting martyrdom, jihad, and paradise premises, keeping its terms and inferential scope stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The strong conclusion is framed conditionally: given the specified metaphysical premises, violent conduct can be instrumentally rational.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The means-end inference is clear and valid once the stated beliefs about martyrdom and immediate paradise are conditionally granted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conditional warrant is strong, but the excerpt does not verify how representative these premises are among relevant actors.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central dogma-and-harm bridge by explaining how religious premises can internally rationalize catastrophic violence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explains a motivational mechanism rather than interpreting a developed opposing alternative, so no meaningful charity test is available.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies martyrdom, jihad, and paradise as premises under which dying in defense of faith becomes instrumentally rational.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Whether religion has evidentiary support is distinct from the practical moral question of which worldview is more likely to produce a good society, a test on which anti-religious secular institutions allegedly failed by overlooking communism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager interrupts to distinguish evidentiary questions from social consequences and then expressly states the comparative argument he is advancing.

components.text: Whether the practical moral performance of a worldview should be assessed separately from evidence for religion.
Whether supernatural authorship claims are adequately supported by evidence.
Whether specified religious premises can make violent conduct internally rational.

response.rationale: Prager expressly separates evidentiary support from the preserved practical issue of producing a good society, justifying that replacement demand while leaving the original evidentiary and motivational claims unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The justified reframe preserves a legitimate comparative moral-performance issue and answers it, though the communism example remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence and practical performance is clear, but good world and anti-religious secular world remain broad and underqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the anti-religious secular world a moral failure on communism exceeds the single asserted historical comparison supplied here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating truth evidence from social consequences is coherent, but the move does not fully bridge one alleged institutional failure to worldview adequacy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical claim about secular failure on communism is asserted without representative institutional evidence, comparison, or causal analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely supports the central social-evil test by proposing practical moral performance as a criterion for worldview assessment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move reframes the issue but does not present a sufficiently developed rival account of secular institutional performance for charity testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager explicitly distinguishes evidence for religion from producing a good world and cites secular institutions' alleged failure regarding communism.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Atheism was not the operative cause of communist, Nazi, or Khmer Rouge atrocities; closed political dogma was the common danger, while open-ended rational inquiry offers a general corrective to unjustified belief.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris rejects the proposed diagnosis, names political dogma as the relevant cause, and answers Prager's direct question about grounding the prohibition on murder.

components.text: Whether atheism or anti-religious secularism is the operative cause of totalitarian atrocities.
Whether secular institutions historically failed to recognize communism as evil.
Whether religious Americans comparatively recognize Islamic totalitarian threats better.

response.rationale: Harris expressly rejects atheism as the diagnosis, identifies closed political dogma as the operative defect, and states open-ended rational inquiry as the corrective consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly attacks the decisive causal inference and supplies a general alternative diagnosis, placing it high within diagnostic defeats.

precisionFindings.rationale: The atheism-versus-dogma diagnosis is recoverable and stable, with an implicit rather than explicit limit on the breadth of dogma claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The alternative diagnosis is plausible and clearly stated, but the universal claim that dogma in any context is the problem is somewhat broader than shown.

charity.alternative: Atheistic or anti-religious commitments materially caused communist and other totalitarian atrocities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Political dogma can coexist with atheism, so correlation alone does not identify atheism as the operative cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal distinction between atheism and closed political dogma is coherent and directly defeats the proposed diagnosis, with one broad generalization remaining.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparative historical diagnosis is reasoned but not documented within the excerpt and does not test mixed or rival causal explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central open-inquiry bridge by contrasting closed dogma with revisable rational inquiry as a corrective.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately engages the causal alternative and supplies the decisive distinction, though it does not examine mixed causal contributions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris rejects atheism as the cause of communist, Nazi, and Khmer Rouge evil and instead identifies closed political dogma.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The existence of persons capable of conversation, together with the existence and apparent design of the world, makes an intentional creator more plausible than treating human and cosmic existence as sheer coincidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager answers Harris's direct question about his belief and supplies a clearly personal, sustained inference from existence and design to a creator.

components.text: Whether there are grounds for believing that an intentional creator exists.
Whether any particular sacred book was written or informed by that creator.
Whether open-ended inquiry corrects unjustified political or religious belief.

response.rationale: The design inference contacts the creator-evidence component of Harris's challenge, but it gives no bridge from a creator to any sacred text and does not address open inquiry.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts a decisive creator component but leaves the scripture-authorship and dogmatic-harm components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The creator inference is recoverable, but coincidence, coming about on its own, creation, and design are treated as interchangeable alternatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that non-design is almost absurd sharply exceeds the supplied observation of existence and omits naturalistic alternatives.

charity.alternative: Human and cosmic existence may arise through nonintentional natural processes rather than sheer coincidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting intentional design does not require treating every causal process as an unexplained pure coincidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference presents design and pure coincidence as the main alternatives, leaving a substantial false-dilemma problem and an unsupported design premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Existence and apparent design are invoked without defending the design judgment or comparing naturalistic causal explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies purported grounds for an intentional creator, placing it high within the central creator-and-scripture tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move reduces the live naturalistic alternative to sheer coincidence and therefore omits its decisive process-based qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager argues from human conversation, worldly existence, and apparent design to a creator while characterizing coincidence as intellectually absurd.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The prohibition on murder remains durable because it rests on divine authority, whereas reliance on discussion alone places unwarranted confidence in fallible human nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly contrasts his divine-command account with Harris's conversational account and states his judgment about their relative rationality.

components.text: Whether open-ended rational inquiry can justify and correct moral beliefs without dogma.
Whether atheism was the operative cause of totalitarian atrocities.
Whether divine or supernatural authority is evidentially supported.

response.rationale: The move asserts divine authority and distrust of human discussion but does not engage Harris's mechanism of open-ended rational correction or his causal diagnosis of totalitarianism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material on moral grounding but remains a nonanswer to the decisive earlier open-inquiry and causal components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The divine-command contrast is clear, but the claim that discussion alone is the secular basis narrows the opposing account without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The durability of the prohibition is attributed to divine speech with certainty, without historical support or comparison to secular mechanisms.

charity.alternative: Secular anti-murder norms can rest on evidence, cooperation, attachment, institutions, and revisable reasoning rather than discussion alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting divine command does not entail confidence that an isolated conversation by itself will restrain human nature.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A divine-command account could explain authority, but the move assumes divine authorship and does not show why the command produces durability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical durability claim and comparison with secular restraint are asserted without evidence, while the divine premise remains undefended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge concerning divine authority and the binding durability of core prohibitions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially weakens the secular alternative by reducing its resources to discussion with a neighbor and generalized faith in humanity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager says the murder prohibition prevails because God said it and contrasts this with discussion and confidence in human nature.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Secular morality can ground concern in the happiness and suffering of conscious creatures and use differences in experiential and neurological capacity to distinguish the interests of humans, animals, embryos, and fetuses.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris answers Prager's challenge directly and repeatedly develops the same capacity-based account despite intervening questions and objections from Prager.

components.text: Whether secular morality has a substantive basis beyond mere discussion or faith in human nature.
Whether human uniqueness or existence supplies evidence for an intentional creator.
Whether a worldview's adequacy should be tested by its contribution to a good society.

response.rationale: Harris identifies conscious happiness and suffering as the omitted secular basis and states that capacity differences yield morally relevant distinctions, defeating the portrayal of secular grounding as mere discussion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly supplies the missing secular ground and its consequence for contested cases, though it does not fully derive every boundary.

precisionFindings.rationale: The account consistently limits concern to creatures capable of experience and explicitly makes moral weight sensitive to degrees of capacity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents capacity as morally relevant while acknowledging questions of degree rather than claiming a fully settled boundary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently links experiential capacity to interests and moral distinctions, though the bridge from capacity to exact comparative weight remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The experiential and neurological framework is relevant, but the excerpt provides no specific developmental evidence or defended weighting rule.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and substantially supports the central conscious-wellbeing bridge by grounding distinctions in happiness, suffering, and capacity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span primarily develops Harris's positive capacity account and does not characterize a sufficiently developed opposing alternative for charity testing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris grounds concern in creatures capable of happiness and suffering and treats the degree of such capacity as morally relevant.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Faith-based certainty that a fully formed soul exists at conception polarizes abortion policy and obstructs nuanced discussion of ethically relevant differences across fetal development.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris identifies polarization as the explanation and attributes it specifically to conception-based soul dogma in a continuous answer to Prager's challenge.

components.text: Whether divine authority is necessary to make core moral prohibitions binding and durable.
Whether human existence and apparent design support belief in an intentional creator.
Whether religious and secular worldviews should be compared by their practical moral results.

response.rationale: The abortion example supplies contrary material about dogma obstructing nuanced inquiry, but it does not contact the decisive divine-authority, creator, or comparative-worldview inferences in the legal targets.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is relevant contrary material about dogmatic effects but a nonanswer to the decisive components of the available earlier targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal thesis is recoverable, but secular people, religious people, and policy discussion are treated broadly without institutional or demographic limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Religious dogmatism is assigned strong causal responsibility for secular discourse failures without comparative evidence or acknowledgment of other causes.

charity.alternative: Conception-based soul beliefs may express concern for continuous human development rather than simply blocking ethical inquiry.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even sincere continuity concerns do not by themselves establish full moral equivalence at every developmental stage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mechanism from fixed soul doctrine to polarization and reduced nuance is plausible, but the broad causal attribution remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The asserted effect on policy discourse is not supported with representative examples, comparative cases, or evidence excluding alternative causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary developmental-distinctions bridge by arguing that dogma blocks attention to ethically relevant fetal development.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies a genuine dogmatic obstacle but does not acknowledge the strongest continuity-based rationale behind the opposing conception view.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris attributes polarized abortion discourse to certainty that a fully formed soul exists at conception and suppresses developmental distinctions.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Ethical realism differs from pragmatism because moral questions can have right and wrong answers grounded in the possible happiness and suffering of conscious physical systems.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris expressly corrects Prager's characterization of realism, defines his own position, and applies it to failures by both secular activists and religious believers.

components.text: Whether the secular account is merely pragmatic rather than a form of moral realism.
Whether divine authority is necessary for objectively right answers about murder.
Whether an intentional creator is the best explanation of human and cosmic existence.

response.rationale: Harris expressly rejects the pragmatist characterization, states that conscious wellbeing admits right and wrong answers, and thereby offers a nondivine source of objective moral judgment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response directly diagnoses the realism-pragmatism conflation and supplies the defeating consequence, while leaving creator evidence aside.

precisionFindings.rationale: The realist proposition and its conscious-system scope are clear, with only an implicit qualification concerning how right answers are discovered.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim of right and wrong answers is clear and bounded, but the excerpt compresses the epistemic warrant for identifying those answers.

charity.alternative: A wellbeing-based account may be pragmatic if it only selects socially useful outcomes rather than objective moral truths.
charity.decisiveQualification: Harris expressly claims truth-apt right and wrong answers, so usefulness alone does not exhaust the proposed standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between realism and pragmatism is coherent, though the inference from wellbeing facts to objective normativity leaves one important bridge implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Conscious happiness and suffering provide relevant subject matter, but the excerpt does not defend the normative bridge or a method for resolving hard cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level secular-grounding bridge by asserting objective moral answers without supernatural premises or sacred texts.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately identifies and directly corrects the strongest live pragmatist interpretation through an explicit realist commitment.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris explicitly opposes realism to pragmatism and locates right and wrong answers in happiness and suffering of conscious physical systems.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The Bible's exceptional moral character supports its divine authorship, and rules that appear primitive in isolation can constitute major moral advances when interpreted within their historical setting.
moves.attributionBasis: The opening row contains the end of Harris's question and the beginning of Prager's answer, after which Prager develops the scriptural argument through the final row.

components.text: Whether sacred scripture has features that provide evidence for divine authorship or moral authority.
Whether scriptural supernatural claims dangerously obstruct responses to present religious extremism.
Whether faith-based certainty obstructs nuanced inquiry into fetal development.
Whether conscious wellbeing supplies objective secular moral answers.

response.rationale: Prager contacts the scripture-evidence demand by invoking exceptional moral character and historical progress, but he leaves the contemporary-harm, abortion, and secular-realism components unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The partial answer reaches a decisive scriptural-evidence component but offers only one compressed historical illustration and misses other targets.

precisionFindings.rationale: Historical-context reasoning is recoverable, but exceptional character and divine authorship are only partly developed in the selected span and remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: One asserted historical advance cannot by itself sustain the broad inference to exceptional moral character or divine authorship.

charity.alternative: Biblical rules can be historical advances relative to their era while still reflecting human moral development rather than divine authorship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative historical progress does not uniquely distinguish divine revelation from ordinary cultural reform.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Historical improvement can answer charges of primitiveness, but the further inference from contextual advance to divine authorship is substantially under-supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The eye-for-an-eye example is asserted as a major advance without developed historical comparison and cannot establish scripture's overall character.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central creator-and-scripture bridge, although much of its developed material also concerns the subsidiary historical-context bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move reasonably insists on historical context but omits the decisive alternative explanation that contextual progress need not imply divine origin.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager offers historical explanation of eye-for-an-eye as moral advancement and presents scriptural moral character as evidence of divine authorship.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Given human attachment, the value placed on cooperation, and the psychological benefits of love and mutual care, societies have secular grounds to reject murder without relying on divine command.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris answers Prager's hypothetical about a person endorsing murder and gives a continuous social and psychological account of why that position fails.

components.text: Whether secular discussion lacks sufficient grounds to sustain the prohibition on murder.
Whether divine authority uniquely explains the prohibition's binding force and durability.
Whether the relevant secular framework can contribute to a viable good society.

response.rationale: Harris identifies attachment, cooperation, love, and social viability as the omitted secular grounds and states the consequence that pro-murder agents cannot sustain happy cooperative life.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly diagnoses the impoverished discussion-only premise and supplies an alternative mechanism with clear social consequences.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cooperation account is clear and stable, with an implicit qualification that it explains social rejection rather than categorical normativity alone.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The prediction that a pro-murder person will find few cooperative partners fits the stated human and social premises, subject to an implicit normal-conditions caveat.

charity.alternative: Divine command may provide categorical authority beyond the prudential and social costs of murder.
charity.decisiveQualification: An account of cooperation can explain convergence and enforcement without fully answering the separate question of categorical obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from human attachment and cooperation to stable rejection of murder is coherent, though categorical wrongness is not fully derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The psychological and cooperative premises are plausible and specific, but the excerpt supplies no representative evidence or treatment of exceptions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly and directly supports the subsidiary cooperation bridge, placing it at the top of the permitted tier range.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly supplies secular resources and defeats the discussion-only framing, though it does not fully resolve divine-command claims about categorical authority.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris appeals to human attachment, cooperation, love, nurturance, and the social isolation facing a person who endorses murder.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: The legal worldview found across Leviticus and Deuteronomy is violently theocratic rather than a dependable timeless moral guide, and later moral progress required societies to outgrow it.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris invites listeners to examine the named biblical legal books and draws an explicit comparative conclusion about their governing worldview and later rejection.

components.text: Whether the biblical legal worldview displays exceptional moral character when read in historical context.
Whether contextual moral advances support an inference to divine authorship.
Whether divine authority reliably secures durable and correct prohibitions on killing.

response.rationale: Harris directly challenges the claimed scriptural character with the legal worldview of Leviticus and Deuteronomy and draws the consequence that later progress required outgrowing it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the decisive scriptural-morality inference with named textual domains and a clear contrary historical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The target texts and theocratic criticism are clear, but claims that killing never stops and the worldview exceeds the Taliban broaden rhetorically.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The named books provide a relevant basis, but the absolute and comparative descriptions exceed the limited textual support presented in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Harsh biblical laws may represent constrained moral advances within an ancient historical environment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Contextual improvement in some rules does not establish the whole legal worldview as timeless or divinely reliable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the named legal corpus is pervasively violent and later rejected, that coherently challenges timeless reliability, though the textual generalization is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Naming Leviticus and Deuteronomy makes the claim testable, but no specific representative laws or contextual comparisons are developed in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central creator-and-scripture bridge by challenging scripture's moral reliability and the inference to divine authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply engages the legal corpus rather than one isolated verse and preserves the decisive whole-worldview qualification, though its Taliban comparison is polemical.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris directs listeners to Leviticus and Deuteronomy, characterizes their legal worldview as violently theocratic, and says it was outgrown.

pro.rationale: No distinct uncaptured debate-wide consequence satisfies the strict residual criteria; all identified effects are already represented in move judgments and burden contacts.

eligibility.distinctConsequence: No distinct residual consequence was identified.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing any alleged residual would not change burden completion independently of the existing move assessments.
